clue.text: Living things turning brown, certainly missing sun

indicators.note: turning round means facing the other way, so the word for brown is read backwards

parts.note: tan is a light brown colour

indicators.note: missing means lacking, so one letter is taken out

parts.note: sure means certainly, as in 'sure, I'll come'
S is the standard abbreviation for sun, as in weather maps and Sunday

explanation.surface: A gardener notes plants turning brown, surely from too little sunshine.
explanation.walkthrough: TAN for 'brown' is turned to NAT; SURE for 'certainly', missing S for sun, leaves URE.
explanation.definitionFit: Nature means the whole world of plants, animals and other living things, as opposed to human works.

clue.text: Organisation receiving articles about stomach in the ape

indicators.note: an organisation that receives something takes it indoors, so its own letters open and close round everything else

parts.note: the everyday three-letter shortening of the word, split to make room

indicators.note: one thing placed about another sits round it, which is where the pair of little words go relative to the stomach

parts.note: the indefinite article twice over, which is why the clue says articles rather than article
gut is the plain word for the stomach, and it goes between that pair

explanation.walkthrough: Phi spells the ape with a final G, the older variant you will find in Chambers; 'articles' being plural is the quiet signal that the same little word appears twice.
explanation.definitionFit: ape -> ORANG-UTANG: the big red tree-dwelling primate of Borneo and Sumatra, so the general word is defined by one of its species.

clue.text: According to Fleming it's M for misbehaviour?

parts.note: the letter at face value, the name given to Bond's boss
the contraction unpacked to 'it is', and only the verb is wanted
in Ian Fleming's novels M runs the Secret Service, so his job title is the word the wordplay wants

explanation.walkthrough: Read the wordplay as a flat statement about who M is in the Bond books and it writes itself out; the question mark covers the joke of 'M for misbehaviour'.
explanation.definitionFit: misbehaviour -> MISCHIEF: playful bad behaviour of the sort children get up to, so the definition is a shade more formal than the answer.

clue.text: Legal establishments showing limits to imagination nonetheless

indicators.note: the limits of a word are where it starts and where it stops, so each word named after this gives up only its two end letters

parts.note: the outside letters of the word, its first and its last
the same treatment applied to the word that follows

explanation.walkthrough: 'Legal establishments' reads at first like licensed premises, which is exactly the pull the setter wants: the Inns of Court are chambers, not bars.
explanation.definitionFit: Legal establishments -> INNS: the four Inns of Court in London are the bodies every English barrister must belong to, so these inns are not pubs.

clue.text: Important naval figure seen in hold?

definitions.meaning: the one-armed admiral who beat the French at Trafalgar in 1805 and stands on the column in the London square named after him
a wrestling grip applied from behind, an arm threaded under the opponent's and the hand pressed on their neck — the full version uses both arms

explanation.walkthrough: The two senses meet only in the spelling, and the question mark is the setter admitting how far apart they are. Capital letter or not is the solver's clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Important naval figure -> Horatio, the admiral of Trafalgar; hold -> the wrestling grip locked round an opponent from behind, two senses sharing one spelling.

clue.text: Nervous European Democrat generally cleared out

parts.note: E is the standard single-letter shortening for European
the American party is reduced to its initial, as on a ballot

indicators.note: a room cleared out keeps its walls and loses its contents, so the word here keeps its two ends and drops the middle

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word, with everything between them gone

explanation.walkthrough: Two of crosswording's commonest one-letter abbreviations sit side by side here; the political surface is decoration, since neither letter depends on which party.
explanation.definitionFit: Nervous -> EDGY: on edge and quick to snap, so the answer carries an irritable streak that plain nervousness does not.

clue.text: Prudent to visit, taking in relative in Holland

indicators.note: taking in means the visit word holds the rest inside it

parts.note: to see someone is to visit them

indicators.note: in places the relative inside the country code

parts.note: NL is the international code for the Netherlands, often called Holland
a sib is a sibling, a relative

explanation.surface: A sensible plan to visit a relative living in the Netherlands.
explanation.definitionFit: Sensible means showing good judgement, which is close to prudent, careful and wise.

clue.text: Attitude after line in retreat

indicators.note: what comes after is written behind, so the attitude follows the line's single letter rather than preceding it

parts.note: L is the standard short form for line
an air is the manner someone carries about them, as in an air of authority

explanation.walkthrough: 'in retreat' reads as one phrase about a beaten army, and that is the trap: 'in' only joins the halves, and 'retreat' on its own is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: retreat -> LAIR: the den an animal withdraws to, so the noun means the place of withdrawal rather than the act of withdrawing.

clue.text: Bar menu not initially ruined — works at possibly dodgy suggestions

parts.note: a bar is a pub, an inn

indicators.note: ruined letters are wrecked and rebuilt in a new order
the word menu loses its opening letter

parts.note: works as a verb: does, as in 'that does the job'

explanation.surface: A diner complains that the pub's food list has been spoiled, and the staff respond with snide remarks.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes 'works' look like a separate comment; it is a verb meaning 'does', and the definition is the final phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Innuendo is a hint or insinuation, often a sly sexual one, hence possibly dodgy remarks.

clue.text: Challenges putting pot in ovens

indicators.note: to put one thing in another is to place it bodily inside, so the pot's letters land in the middle of the longer word

parts.note: to face a difficulty is to challenge it head on, and this is the outer word
an urn is a big pot, for ashes or for tea, and it goes within

explanation.walkthrough: 'Challenges' at the head of the clue looks like the definition; it is the container instead, and the plural 'ovens' at the end is what the answer must match.
explanation.definitionFit: ovens -> FURNACES: a furnace is an enclosed fire fierce enough to smelt metal, so the definition names it by its domestic cousin.

clue.text: Mum certainly tense — most likely to withdraw

parts.note: mum means keeping quiet, and SH is the noise that asks for it
answer certainly to a question and you have said yes
T is the grammarian's short form for tense, as in past T

explanation.walkthrough: The dash marks the seam: everything before it builds the word and everything after defines it. 'Mum' is the silence sense, nothing to do with mothers.
explanation.definitionFit: most likely to withdraw -> SHYEST: the shyest person is the one who hangs back hardest from company, so the superlative answers 'most'.

clue.text: Particular probe gutted by copper taking on unreliable source

indicators.note: to take something on is to add it to what you already carry, so the letters that follow join the end
a gutted building keeps its shell and loses its insides, so only the first and last letters of the word survive

parts.note: the outside letters of probe, with its middle emptied out
the chemical symbol for copper, from the Latin cuprum
a source who cannot be relied on is a liar, and that is the whole of this piece

explanation.walkthrough: The surface offers a detective leaning on a dubious informant, and every word of it is doing some other job — 'copper' here is the metal, not the policeman.
explanation.definitionFit: Particular -> PECULIAR: both mean belonging to one person or thing alone — a peculiar habit is one particular to you, not merely an odd one.

clue.text: Bounders impounding river ferries

indicators.note: to impound something is to shut it up in a pound, so the animals keep the river shut inside them

parts.note: roos are kangaroos, the animals that get about by bounding
R is the map-maker's abbreviation for river, as in R. Thames

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bounders' first reads as cads out of P. G. Wodehouse, and that is the misdirection: these bounders are animals that bound.
explanation.definitionFit: ferries -> RO-ROS: a ro-ro is a roll-on/roll-off ship that vehicles drive straight aboard and off again, so the plural names a type of boat.

clue.text: Head back round South, ending in legendary battleground

indicators.note: the reversed head goes round the South letter, holding it
going back means the word for head is read in reverse

parts.note: bean is slang for the head
S is the compass abbreviation for South

indicators.note: only the last letter of legendary is used

parts.note: its last letter is Y

explanation.surface: Someone heads back around the South to a legendary battlefield.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Legendary' reads as describing the battleground, but it only supplies its final letter; Naseby was the decisive English Civil War battle of 1645.
explanation.definitionFit: Naseby in Northamptonshire was the site of the 1645 battle where Parliament beat Charles I.

clue.text: Yahoo menu's edited? I thought that was very bad

definitions.text: I thought that was very bad

indicators.note: an editor cuts and reorders what is on the page, so the letters do not stay in the order they were handed over

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.walkthrough: A yahoo is a lout, Swift's word from Gulliver's Travels, so the surface reads as a complaint about a website while the capital letter does nothing at all.
explanation.definitionFit: I thought that was very bad -> SHAME ON YOU: the set phrase you say to condemn someone's behaviour, so a whole sentence defines a whole phrase.

clue.text: Meteorological measure is absolute farce in a storm

indicators.note: letters caught in a storm get blown out of their places, and a storm is also what the answer exists to measure

parts.note: anagram fodder, thirteen letters

explanation.walkthrough: Rear Admiral Francis Beaufort drew the scale up for the Royal Navy in 1805, and the anagram indicator naming the very thing being measured is the clue's joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Meteorological measure -> BEAUFORT SCALE: the 0-to-12 wind scale, calm to hurricane, by which forecasters and sailors describe how hard it is blowing.

clue.text: B_____ fool almost cut through item on score

parts.note: an insult bowdlerised down to its first letter, and that letter is all the wordplay hands over
an ass is a fool, the donkey standing in for the idiot

indicators.note: almost there means stopping just short, so the word gives up the letter it would have finished on

parts.note: something cut through has been cleft, and the past participle is the word to trim

explanation.walkthrough: The row of dashes is the joke and the wordplay at once: a paper printing a word it will not print leaves you the initial, and the initial is what the clue needs.
explanation.definitionFit: item on score -> BASS CLEF: the curled sign at the start of a stave that fixes where the low notes sit, so it is a mark written on music.

clue.text: Odd crime newspaper picked up, involving university lecturer

parts.note: a sin is a wrongdoing, a crime against morality

indicators.note: the reversed newspaper takes in the other letters
in a down clue picking up means reading from bottom to top

parts.note: a rag is a disparaging word for a newspaper

explanation.surface: A strange crime in which a tabloid gets mixed up with a university lecturer.
explanation.definitionFit: Singular can mean strange or peculiar, as in a singular occurrence.

clue.text: Our group adds wrinkles to ways of working

parts.note: the pronoun for the group that includes whoever is speaking
what ages a face puts wrinkles on it, so the verb does the same work

explanation.walkthrough: 'Adds wrinkles' is a verb phrase dressed up as skincare copy; the answer is a plural noun, which is the test of whether the definition really fits.
explanation.definitionFit: ways of working -> USAGES: a usage is an established custom or practice, so the plural covers the accepted ways a thing is habitually done.

clue.text: High-pitched soprano damaging after brief time

indicators.note: the damaging word comes after the hour

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for soprano in music
HR is the short form of hour
ill can mean harmful or damaging, as in ill effects

explanation.surface: A soprano's voice turns harmful after a short spell.
explanation.definitionFit: A shrill sound is piercing and high in pitch.

clue.text: More reasonable about bringing in college's white wine

indicators.note: to bring something in is to fetch it inside, so the college letter ends up within the word before it

parts.note: saner is the comparative of sane, reasonable in the plain sense
C is the abbreviation for college as it appears in institution names
RE means about or concerning, as at the head of a memo

explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like an instruction to wrap one piece round another, and it is a piece of the answer instead — RE, the word at the top of a memo.
explanation.definitionFit: white wine -> SANCERRE: a crisp Sauvignon Blanc from the upper Loire, so the answer is one named example of what the definition describes.

clue.text: Haphazard components of read-only memory

parts.note: read-only memory shortens to ROM, and this is the first of the three letters it is made of
list a set of components aloud and an 'and' goes in before the last of them, which is where these three letters come from
the other two letters of that same abbreviation, in the order they come

explanation.walkthrough: ROM is the memory chip that keeps its contents when the power goes off. The trick is that the clue wants its letters read out as a list rather than as an abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Haphazard -> RANDOM: both describe something with no plan behind it, though haphazard hints at carelessness where the answer is neutral.

clue.text: Cake — first answer provided by every cook at the outset

indicators.note: the answer word is supplied by, so follows, the opening letters
at the outset means at the start, so the first letter of each word is taken

parts.note: their first letters are E and C
the first answer in this puzzle is 8 Across, LAIR

explanation.surface: A recipe note: every cook should first supply the answer for a cake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first answer' points to the grid: 8 Across is the first clue, a cross-reference rather than a word to define.
explanation.definitionFit: An eclair is a long choux pastry cake filled with cream and topped with chocolate.

clue.text: Hearts absorbed by cool desire

indicators.note: what is absorbed vanishes into whatever takes it up, so the card suit's letter ends up within the other word

parts.note: ace means excellent or cool in everyday slang, and it is the outer word
H is the card player's abbreviation for hearts

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves come from games — a card suit's initial and the top card standing in for 'cool' — while the surface sells you a romance.
explanation.definitionFit: desire -> ACHE: to ache for something is to want it painfully, so this is longing with a hurt in it rather than plain wanting.

clue.text: Regretting our name being appropriated by China

indicators.note: what is appropriated is taken and kept by the taker, so these letters finish up held inside the porcelain word

parts.note: the Chinese dynasty whose porcelain the word china is named for, so the capital letter is a disguise
the pronoun at face value, three letters as written
N is the standard abbreviation for name

explanation.walkthrough: China is the crockery, not the country, and the dynasty that made it is the piece to find. The capital letter is the setter's licence and the whole of the disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: Regretting -> MOURNING: mourning is grief for something lost, so it is regret at its deepest, and formal enough to be worn rather than merely felt.

clue.text: Lots of people, some upsetting bird

indicators.note: upsetting a word knocks its letters out of place, so they are rearranged

parts.note: many, used as a pronoun, means lots of people

explanation.surface: A remark that a crowd, or some of it, finds something distressing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upsetting' rearranges MANY; 'some' merely softens the surface and does no work.
explanation.definitionFit: The myna is an Asian starling famous for mimicking human speech, kept as a cage bird.

clue.text: I will enter a chapel on rocky Greek island

indicators.note: what enters goes in among the rest, so the single letter joins the pile being shuffled instead of standing outside it
a rocky road is uneven and unsteady, and letters given a rocky ride do not stay in the order they arrived in

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters
the tenth letter, joining the fodder before the shuffle

explanation.walkthrough: 'on' belongs to the letters, not to the picture of a chapel standing on a hill — which is why the fodder counts out to ten and not nine.
explanation.definitionFit: Greek island -> CEPHALONIA: the largest of the Ionian islands, off the west coast of Greece, so a named place answers a general description.

clue.text: Old tidal wave eliminating river reed

parts.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old

indicators.note: to eliminate something is to get rid of it, so the letter named next is struck out of the word before

parts.note: a bore is the wave that runs up a river on a rising tide, as on the Severn
R is the map's short form for river, and it is the letter struck out

explanation.walkthrough: The Severn bore is a real tidal wave that surfers ride miles upstream, which is how 'tidal wave' and 'river' can sit side by side so innocently.
explanation.definitionFit: reed -> OBOE: the woodwind whose sound is made by a double reed, so the definition names the instrument by the part that voices it.
